title: What training does OSHA require for mechanical power press operators and machine guarding?
description: OSHA 1910.217 power press training: operator instruction under (f)(2), maintenance competence, PSDI annual training and certification, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) mechanical power press standard, 29 CFR 1910.217(f)(2), requires employers to train and instruct each operator in the safe method of work before starting any covered operation and to confirm through adequate supervision that correct procedures are followed. Paragraph (e)(3) requires the original and continuing competence of maintenance and inspection personnel. Presses used in presence sensing device initiation (PSDI) mode add annual operator training with a certification record kept for the duration of employment.
keyTakeaways: Paragraph (f)(2) requires operator training before work starts and ongoing supervision, but sets no fixed refresher interval and no certification for conventional presses.

Presses used in PSDI mode require operator training before first operation, as needed to maintain competence, and not less than annually, with a certification record kept for the duration of employment.
Employers must ensure the original and continuing competence of personnel who care for, inspect and maintain power presses.
Press brakes, hydraulic and pneumatic presses, forging presses and several other machines are excluded from 1910.217 and fall under the general machine guarding rule in 1910.212.
Machine guarding (29 CFR 1910.212) was tenth in OSHA's preliminary list of most cited standards for fiscal year 2026.
jurisdiction: United States (federal, with state plan variations)
regulator: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), US Department of Labor
appliesTo: Manufacturers and metalworking shops operating mechanical power presses covered by 29 CFR 1910.217
Press operators, die setters, and personnel who care for, inspect and maintain power presses
Employers using presses in presence sensing device initiation (PSDI) mode
All general industry employers with machines that require guarding under 29 CFR 1910.212

sections.heading: Which machines does the power press standard cover?

blocks.text: The standard at [29 CFR 1910.217](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1910.217) covers mechanical power presses. Paragraph (a)(5) excludes press brakes, hydraulic and pneumatic power presses, bulldozers, hot bending and hot metal presses, forging presses and hammers, riveting machines and similar fastener applicators.

Excluded machines are not unregulated. They fall under the general machine guarding requirement in [29 CFR 1910.212](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1910.212), which requires one or more methods of guarding to protect the operator and other employees from hazards such as the point of operation, ingoing nip points, rotating parts, flying chips and sparks. Section 1910.212 sets guarding duties but contains no training paragraph, so operator training for excluded machines is driven by the employer's own procedures, OSHA's general duty clause, and related standards such as lockout/tagout.

sections.heading: What does paragraph (f)(2) require for press operator training?

blocks.text: Paragraph (f)(2) is short and outcome based. It states: "The employer shall train and instruct the operator in the safe method of work before starting work on any operation covered by this section. The employer shall insure by adequate supervision that correct operating procedures are being followed."

Three practical consequences follow. First, training is tied to the operation, so a new die, feeding method or safeguarding arrangement is a new operation that needs instruction in its safe method. Second, training alone is not enough: the employer must supervise to confirm procedures are followed. Third, there is no certification or fixed refresher requirement for conventional presses in (f)(2), so the evidence is the employer's own record of who was instructed in which operation and how supervision is carried out.

Several other provisions shape what that training should cover. Paragraph (f)(4) requires presses to be operated within the manufacturer's tonnage and attachment weight ratings, and paragraph (f)(3) requires clearance between machines and floors free from obstructions, grease, oil and water. Two-hand controls and trips must be fixed so that only a supervisor or safety engineer can relocate them, and stroking mode selection must be capable of supervision by the employer.

sections.heading: What competence is required for press maintenance and inspection personnel?

blocks.text: Paragraph (e)(3) makes the employer responsible for "the original and continuing competence of personnel caring for, inspecting, and maintaining power presses." The word continuing means a one-off course does not settle the duty.

The inspection program in paragraph (e)(1) shows what that competence must support. The general component requires periodic and regular inspection of each press, including the clutch/brake mechanism, antirepeat feature and single-stroke mechanism, with a certification record of each inspection, maintenance and repair task that shows the date, the signature of the person who did the work and the press identifier. The directed component requires inspection and testing of the clutch/brake mechanism, antirepeat feature and single-stroke mechanism at least once a week, with certification records for maintenance tasks performed.

Because the inspection certifications carry the signature of the person who performed the work, auditors can check each signature against the competence record. Die setting and press maintenance usually also bring [lockout/tagout training](/regulations/osha-lockout-tagout-training-requirements) duties, since the minor servicing exception in that standard applies only where alternative measures give effective protection.

sections.heading: What extra training applies to presses used in PSDI mode?

blocks.text: Presence sensing device initiation lets a light curtain both safeguard and start the press stroke, and paragraph (h) adds stricter training rules for it. Under paragraph (h)(13)(i), the operator training required by (f)(2) must be provided before the employee first operates the press, "as needed to maintain competence, but not less than annually thereafter."

The PSDI training must cover five items: the manufacturer's recommended test procedures for checking the presence sensing device, including use of the test rod; the safety distance required; the operation, function and performance of the PSDI mode; the requirements for hand tools that may be used; and the severe consequences of attempting to circumvent or bypass any safeguard or operating function.

Paragraph (h)(13)(ii) requires a certification record with the identity of the person trained, the signature of the employer or trainer, and the date training was completed. It must be prepared at the end of training, kept on file for the duration of the employee's employment, and made available to OSHA on request. Paragraph (h)(10)(vi) separately requires initial and periodic training for personnel who care for, inspect and maintain PSDI presses, and under paragraph (h)(11)(ii) the PSDI safety system must be recertified by the employer and revalidated by an OSHA-recognized third-party validation organization at least annually.

sections.heading: What happens when a press operator is injured?

blocks.text: Point-of-operation injuries on mechanical power presses must be reported within 30 days. Paragraph (g)(1) requires the employer to report all point-of-operation injuries to operators or other employees to OSHA's Directorate of Standards and Guidance, or to the state plan agency.

The report must include the task being performed, the clutch type, the safeguards in use, the cause of the accident, the type of feeding, the means used to actuate the stroke, and the number of operators required and provided with controls and safeguards. Those fields map closely to what operator training should address, so each report is a natural input to a training review.

sections.heading: How often is machine guarding cited?

blocks.text: Machine guarding is a perennial enforcement priority. OSHA's [preliminary top 10 for fiscal year 2026](https://www.osha.gov/top10citedstandards) lists the general machine guarding requirements in 1910.212 tenth across all industries. Penalty ceilings for violations assessed after January 15, 2026 are on [OSHA's penalties page](https://www.osha.gov/penalties).

Plants that run presses usually manage several overlapping OSHA training duties at once. An overview is in [OSHA training requirements](/regulations/osha-training-requirements), and the quality system side of press competence for automotive suppliers is covered in [IATF 16949 competence and awareness](/regulations/iatf-16949-competence-and-awareness-requirements).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry structures press training per operation, linking each die and safeguarding setup to its safe method of work and to the operators instructed on it. For PSDI presses, the five required topics become assessment points with an annual cycle and a certification record held for the life of employment.

faqs.q: Does OSHA require certification for mechanical power press operators?
faqs.a: Only for presses used in PSDI mode. Paragraph (h)(13)(ii) requires a certification record for PSDI operator training, kept for the duration of employment. For conventional presses, paragraph (f)(2) requires training, instruction and adequate supervision, but no certification. Employers should still keep records showing who was trained on which operation.

faqs.q: How often must power press operators be retrained?
faqs.a: Paragraph (f)(2) sets no fixed interval for conventional presses; training is required before each covered operation, and supervision must confirm correct procedures. Presses in PSDI mode require training as needed to maintain competence and at least annually.

faqs.q: Are hydraulic presses and press brakes covered by 1910.217?
faqs.a: No. Paragraph (a)(5) excludes press brakes, hydraulic and pneumatic presses, forging presses and hammers, hot bending and hot metal presses, bulldozers, and riveting machines. Those machines are subject to the general machine guarding requirements in 1910.212, which require guarding but contain no separate training paragraph.

faqs.q: Does machine guarding training count as lockout/tagout training?
faqs.a: No. Guarding protects during normal production, while lockout/tagout covers servicing and maintenance. Clearing a jam that requires bypassing a guard or reaching into the point of operation generally brings the lockout/tagout standard and its separate training requirements into play.
